Summary

ASTER — Abandoned But Not Forgotten is an interactive webcomic that connects a fictional future expedition with the real history of space exploration. Across three chapters, Mara, Eli, and their robot companion Pip encounter equipment left on the Moon and Mars, including the Apollo 11 landing site and the Sojourner rover.

Through illustrated scenes, dialogue, archival photographs, mission timelines, and interactive activities, readers discover what these missions achieved and why their legacy still matters. NASA resources provide the historical foundation, while our original story makes that information approachable and emotionally engaging.

The project addresses the challenge by giving forgotten space hardware a place in a new story without presenting fiction as documented history. Designed for desktop and mobile browsers, ASTER aims to encourage curiosity about science, respect for space heritage, and appreciation of the people and machines that made later exploration possible.
details:
Project Details

ASTER — Abandoned But Not Forgotten is a browser-based interactive webcomic about the legacy of space exploration. Our central idea is that equipment left on another world is more than an abandoned object: it represents discoveries, engineering achievements, and the people who made future exploration possible.

HOW THE PROJECT WORKS

Readers follow Mara, Eli, and their robot companion Pip through three connected chapters. Their fictional journey takes them from Earth to the Moon and Mars, where they encounter the traces of earlier missions.

The experience combines illustrated environments, character dialogue, camera movement, sound, historical photographs, and interactive activities. Readers can explore historical information, examine mission timelines, and take control of Sojourner in an educational rover activity.

The story introduces real missions including Apollo 11, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance. The lunar archive also includes the Apollo laser retroreflector, Lunar Roving Vehicles, and Lunokhod 1.

NASA mission resources and archival images provide the factual foundation. The future expedition, its characters, and the recovery of Sojourner belong to our fictional narrative. Interactive scientific visualizations, such as the APXS spectrum, are illustrative rather than actual instrument measurements.

PURPOSE AND INTENDED IMPACT

We want to make space history approachable for students, younger audiences, and people who may not normally read technical mission reports. Our project combines curiosity and emotion: readers first connect with the characters, then discover the real achievements behind the objects they encounter.

ASTER responds to the challenge by turning equipment left behind into a meaningful part of a new story. It encourages appreciation of scientific heritage and shows how successive missions build on earlier work. These are intended educational benefits; we have not conducted a formal study measuring learning outcomes.

ORIGINAL WORK AND CREATIVE APPROACH

Our team created the story from scratch, including the characters, their personalities, relationships, and narrative roles. We established the artistic direction and drew the original visual references for Mara and Eli.

Pip and the spacecraft were also conceived by our team, but their illustrations were produced with SI assistance rather than drawn entirely by hand. Our team developed the mini-game concepts and their place within the story.

The creative approach combines an original character-driven narrative with documented mission history. Instead of presenting the material only as a list of facts, we connect historical discoveries to moments of exploration, humor, reflection, and care.

TECHNOLOGY AND IMPLEMENTATION

The website was built with React, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS, using Vite for development and production builds. GSAP coordinates scene animation, camera movement, and transitions. Browser audio code using the Web Audio API produces character voice blips, sound cues, and ambient music.

Git and GitHub were used for version control, and the website is deployed on Vercel. It runs in a web browser without requiring installation or specialized hardware.

The implementation includes chapter selection, dialogue controls, pause and sound settings, historical information panels, responsive layouts, and reduced-motion support. We considered screen size, text readability, interaction timing, visual consistency, loading performance, and the distinction between historical information and fiction.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used SI tools as production assistants and disclose their contribution separately from our team's original creative work.

OpenAI Codex and Anthropic's Claude through Claude Code helped write and refine website code, including the story player, interactive activities, scene transitions, responsive layouts, animations, temporary placeholder graphics, and bug fixes.

ChatGPT helped structure development requests and draft explanatory project text.

Generative image tools helped create backgrounds and additional character poses based on our references and artistic direction. OpenAI image generation was used for the painted space background and Pip's pose carrying Sojourner. Image-editing assistance also helped prepare the team-supplied logo for the website.

We do not claim that all artwork was hand-drawn or that all code was written without SI assistance. Historical facts come from credited source materials, not from generated fiction. Generated illustrations are artistic interpretations, not NASA photographs or mission records.

SOURCES AND ATTRIBUTION

NASA mission information and imagery are listed in NASA Data. Materials from other providers are listed separately, including the Wikimedia Commons photograph of the Lunokhod 1 model and Natural Earth coastline geometry used in a fallback Earth illustration.

Third-party code and font resources are identified separately from scientific data. The website includes Credits & Sources and Project Details to explain attribution and authorship. NASA does not endorse this project.
